title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to take George Eliot's great novel apart — passage by passage, argument by argument — and put it back together again.

The Mill on the Floss is a novel about belonging and exclusion, about families that bind and families that wound, about a girl whose intelligence and feeling outrun every structure her world offers her.
It is also one of the funniest, most heartbreaking, most formally brilliant novels in the English language.
To unpick all of that, I have three remarkable readers with me today.
First, Dr Eleanor Hartley — a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed, in the best possible way, with how great fiction actually works from the inside.
Eleanor has a gift for making the technical feel thrilling — she will be our guide to the architecture of Eliot's sentences and the craft beneath the emotion.
Then, Dr Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian who reads novels as X-rays of class power.
Daniel will be asking who the novel's institutions serve, who they crush, and what George Eliot — perhaps more than she knew — was saying about the society she lived in.
And finally, Ms Caroline Woodcourt — a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Caroline is our guide to the experience of reading — what makes you stop, re-read, catch your breath, or quietly weep on public transport.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin where the novel insists we must — with fate, with family, and with what it means to be caught in a current you did not choose.
What strikes me first about The Mill on the Floss — even before the great set pieces — is the narrator's voice.
Eliot builds her world on this extraordinary tension between sympathy and irony — she loves her characters and she sees through them, simultaneously.
And nowhere is that clearer than in how she handles Tulliver's fate.
There's a moment early in the novel where Tulliver has sworn he will never do business with Wakem's clients.
Within a fortnight, he has done exactly that — not, Eliot tells us, because his will was weak, but because external fact was stronger.
And then she delivers this:
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
That is an astonishing move.
She invokes Greek tragedy — the grandest possible frame — for a provincial miller borrowing money from the wrong man.
It is comic and tragic at once, which is precisely Tulliver's condition.
That Oedipus comparison is doing more than elevating a small man to tragic dignity, though — and I think Eliot knows it.
The deeper point is about how market forces produce the appearance of destiny.
Tulliver has no real choice because capital in St Ogg's has already consolidated around Wakem.
The "external fact" that defeats him isn't fate in the cosmic sense — it's monopoly.
What Eliot is showing us — and this runs through the whole novel — is a world in which the law and money and respectability all converge in the same hands.
And those hands belong to Wakem.
What I love about that passage is the sheer cheek of it.
Eliot is genuinely fond of Tulliver — you feel that — and yet she won't let him off the hook.
She names his delusion exactly as it is, and then she forgives it by framing it as destiny.
That's the thing about re-reading this novel — you keep noticing how the narrator holds two completely contradictory attitudes at the same moment.
It's one of the reasons the book stays so alive.
And that double attitude is exactly what Eliot brings to bear on the children too — particularly Maggie.
There's a passage I keep returning to — the scene after Tom confronts Maggie about Philip, and she goes up to her room.
Eliot renders Maggie's inner state with this almost unbearable precision:
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict.
And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions."
That phrase — "serene heights" — is doing something architecturally brilliant.
It echoes the renunciation chapters, where Maggie believed she had transcended desire — and now the whole edifice collapses in a single sentence.
Reading that passage aloud is almost physically difficult.
Because Eliot doesn't stop at the fall — she then gives us this:

"Her heart bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
That image — beating the floor, tightening the fingers — isn't decorative.
It's the body registering what the mind cannot process — empathy so acute it becomes indistinguishable from pain.
I find it almost unbearable, every single time.
What interests me is what's producing that pain — because it doesn't arrive in a vacuum.
Tom has just told Philip — told him to his face — exactly what the world thinks of a deformed boy from a lawyer's family courting a miller's daughter.
The cruelty isn't personal spite — it's the voice of the whole social order speaking through Tom.
Listen to what he actually says:
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you,—from making herself a laughing-stock,—from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son.
You know well enough what sort of justice and cherishing you were preparing for her."
"Justice and cherishing" — that is a devastating piece of sarcasm.
Tom is using the language of protection and honour to perform exactly the class violence he claims to be shielding Maggie from.
And the terrible thing is — he believes every word of it.
That's what makes Tom such a difficult character to hold in your head.
He's not a villain — he's a system.
And Eliot builds him from the inside with the same patience and sympathy she gives Maggie — which is what makes it so crushing.
Destiny, class, empathy, cruelty — and we're barely out of the opening.
That sense of forces converging on characters who are simultaneously fully human and utterly trapped — that is the Mill on the Floss in a sentence.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at how Eliot constructs the world those characters inhabit — the landscapes, the institutions, and the particular cruelty of provincial life.

segments.title: The Weight of Failure: Tulliver's Ruin and Class

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we are deep inside one of the great English novels — George Eliot's portrait of a family undone by pride, law, and the merciless logic of Victorian commerce.

Our segment today is called The Weight of Failure — we're looking at the Tulliver ruin: what causes it, what it costs, and what it reveals about the class machinery humming underneath this novel's surface.
Joining me are three extraordinary readers of this book.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who reads fiction the way a watchmaker reads a watch — always after the mechanism behind the beauty.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees every drawing room and every ledger book in a novel as a site of class power — and he is rarely wrong.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager and brings an irreplaceable reader's intimacy to everything she touches.
Let's begin with the moment that sets the ruin in motion — Mr Tulliver's extraordinary letter to Mrs Glegg.
What strikes me first about that letter scene is the comic architecture Eliot builds around it.
She opens by telling us Mrs Glegg is wallowing in the warm bath of her own magnanimity — she has just decided to be the generous one, to forgive.
And then, into that self-satisfied moment, Eliot drops Tulliver's letter like a cold stone into still water.
The narrator sets it up with almost theatrical relish — listen to this.
"she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
That phrase — 'he desired no favours' — is Tulliver at his most magnificently, catastrophically proud.
He is refusing exactly what would save him, and he is doing it with almost formal courtesy — which makes it funnier and sadder at once.
And behind that pride, Daniel, there is something much more structural at work — isn't there?
Absolutely — and I think Eleanor puts her finger on exactly the right word: pride.
But pride, in this novel, is never simply personal vanity.
It is the psychological armour of a man whose class position is already precarious, who feels the ground shifting under him and responds by standing more rigidly upright.
What I want to bring in here is the narrator's extraordinary account of what actually drives Tulliver into the lawsuit — because it is not simply hot-headedness.
Eliot gives us this passage about Mrs Tulliver's 'monotonous pleading' — and this is where her satirical blade is sharpest.
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back"
But Eliot immediately corrects herself — the blame lies not with that final feather but with all the previous weight.
That weight is structural: debt, the law, the slow erosion of a small miller's independence in a world run by people like Wakem.
What moves me in that passage — and it is both funny and painful — is that Mrs Tulliver's influence works precisely because she is seen as a Dodson, not as herself.
Eliot says he sees in her 'the representative of the Dodson family' — her individual voice is erased.
She is always a category to him, never quite a person.
And then there is the Wakem obsession — which Eliot renders in this glorious ventriloquism of Tulliver's paranoid interior.
She sets it up and then gives us this — absolutely unforgettable.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
You hear Tulliver's voice so directly there — the sputtering indignation, the almost physical revulsion.
It is free indirect discourse doing its finest work — we are inside the prejudice, inhabiting it, even as Eliot holds it at arm's length.
Caroline is absolutely right about the free indirect discourse — and I'd add that what makes it so devastating is that Eliot does not let Tulliver off the hook.
She lets us feel the warmth of his conviction, his certainty that Wakem is a rascal — and then she quietly notes that his own lawyer Gore is probably not up to the fight.
There is a brilliant structural irony there: the man most consumed by the fantasy of legal victory is the man least equipped to achieve it.

The whole passage about Wakem — 'all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem's rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver's interests' — is Eliot showing us how ideology works.
The particular and the universal collapse into one — Tulliver's grievance becomes cosmic justice.
And Eliot makes sure we understand what the ruin actually costs — not in abstract terms, but in the most material, intimate way possible.
The scene where Mrs Tulliver goes through her linens is one of the most quietly devastating in the whole novel.
She is not an intellectual woman — Eliot has been lightly satirical about her — but in this moment she becomes the novel's truest voice of loss.
Listen to how Eliot renders her speech.

"To think o' these cloths as I spun myself... and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back, as I remember standing at the door and seeing him come, before I ever thought o' marrying your father!"
That memory of standing at the door — before marriage, before the mill, before the ruin — carries everything.
These cloths are not just property — they are labour, time, identity, hope.
When they are sold, it is not merely an economic event — it is the erasure of a life's making.

I find that scene almost unbearable on re-reading, because Eliot shows Mrs Tulliver at her most animated — 'the excitement all the more strange and piteous because the stout blond woman was usually so passive.'
This is the one moment where her inner life overflows — and it overflows over linen.
Which tells you something devastating about what her life has permitted her to invest herself in.
And that line to Tom — 'You'll never have one of 'em, my boy' — just breaks me every time.
She had planned a future that is now impossible, and the linen was the material form of that plan.
And this is where I want to bring in the Dodson code, because it is the ideological context that makes the ruin so total.
Eliot gives us one of her great set pieces — the anatomy of Dodson religion and respectability — and it is satire so precise it reads like anthropology.
She writes — and this is the line I keep returning to.

"Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it,—if heresy properly means choice,—for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
'Like asthma' — that parenthetical is almost shockingly funny, and yet the point underneath it is serious.
These people do not choose their values any more than they choose a hereditary illness — the values are simply the air they breathe.
And the core of that value system — 'to be honest and rich, and not only rich, but richer than was supposed' — makes the Tulliver ruin not just a personal catastrophe but a kind of excommunication.
What I admire technically in that passage is how Eliot manages to be inside the Dodson worldview and outside it simultaneously.
She genuinely concedes their virtues — 'society owes some worthy qualities in many of her members to mothers of the Dodson class' — that is not ironic.
But she also sees, with perfect clarity, what happens when that code becomes the whole of moral life: it leaves no room for the kind of sympathy that could absorb failure.
The Dodsons will not let you want bread — but they will make you eat it with bitter herbs.
And that is precisely what Tom does to Maggie — he becomes the Dodson code made flesh.
The scene where he demands she swear on the Bible is one of the most wrenching in the novel — because Tom is not a villain.
He has worked himself to the bone for the family.
And yet hear what he says to Maggie — the charge he levels against her.
"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you."
And then — this is the sentence that undoes me — he connects his own sacrifice directly to her alleged betrayal.
"while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both"
Respectability — that is the word that carries everything Tom believes in, and everything that crushes Maggie.
Tom is the Dodson code's most devoted servant — and also its most tragic product.
He has paid the family's debts through sheer disciplined labour — which the novel genuinely respects.
But the currency in which he demands repayment from Maggie is compliance — total, sworn, bodily compliance.
He asks her to put her hand on the Bible and speak a formula of renunciation — to perform obedience as a ritual.
That is the Dodson religion in its purest form: propriety enacted as ceremony, without any examined inner life.
And what Eliot has constructed across these chapters is a kind of tragedy of systems — no single villain, no single failure.
Tulliver's pride, the law's indifference, the Dodson code's rigidity, Tom's sacrificial fury — they all press on Maggie simultaneously.
And what is remarkable — what is Eliot's real genius here — is that each of these forces has its own coherent logic.
None of them is simply wrong — they are all simultaneously right and crushing.
That phrase — 'right and crushing' — feels like the perfect note on which to pause.
We've traced the ruin from its comic origins in Tulliver's pride, through the material devastation of the linen sale, to the ideological prison that Tom enforces on Maggie.
In our next segment, we'll be asking what Eliot offers as an alternative — whether the novel imagines any escape from the weight it has so carefully described.
Stay with us.
Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into one of the novel's most compelling subjects: Maggie Tulliver's mind.
Her hunger — intellectual, emotional, imaginative — and the walls that keep closing in around her.
Joining me today are three readers who each bring something distinct and vital to this conversation.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great gift is showing us how George Eliot builds her effects — sentence by sentence, image by image.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads the novel as an anatomy of class and power — and who insists, compellingly, that Eliot was more radical than she knew.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite let it go — she's our guide to what it feels like to live inside these pages.
Let's begin with Maggie as a child — those extraordinary early chapters where Eliot is already mapping the full shape of her character.
What strikes me every time I return to these chapters is how completely George Eliot inhabits Maggie's emotional logic.
The jealousy Maggie feels over Tom's attention to Lucy — it's rendered with such precision that it feels almost uncomfortable to read.
Because Eliot doesn't soften it or excuse it.
There's this passage I keep coming back to, where we see exactly how Maggie's affection curdles under pressure.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
That image — the white mouse — it's so tender, and Eliot places it right next to Maggie's violent fantasy of slapping Lucy.
The cruelty Maggie imagines isn't monstrous — it's heartbreakingly ordinary.
And notice what Eliot is doing structurally in that passage — she gives us the moral before the sin.
We're told what Maggie would have thought, the better version of herself, before we're shown the darker impulse crowding in.
That gap — between who Maggie wants to be and what she's actually feeling — that gap is the engine of the whole novel.
And it's Tom who creates the gap here — his preference for Lucy converts Lucy from a beloved cousin into a rival.
What I love is the parenthetical precision: it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.
"it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her"
That little aside carries a whole social world — the labour of affection, and who is expected to perform it.
Eleanor's right, and I'd push it further.
What Eliot is encoding in that throwaway phrase — it had been left to Maggie — is the entire structure of emotional labour assigned to girls.
Tom can withdraw his care as soon as it's inconvenient.
Maggie cannot — until she fantasises about slapping Lucy, which is the only form of refusal available to her.
And even that fantasy is immediately channelled through Tom — she wants to vex him, not liberate herself.
Which brings us to the moment when Maggie does refuse — when she decides to run away to the gypsies.
It's one of the most delightful and quietly devastating passages in the novel.
I love this passage so much.
There is something so perfectly observed about the way Maggie escalates her own misery until it demands a dramatic solution.
Eliot tells us: she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense that this was a great crisis in her life.
"she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense that this was a great crisis in her life"
The comedy and the pathos are absolutely inseparable there.
It is a great crisis — just not quite in the way Maggie thinks.
And then the plan to send her father a letter by a small gypsy — I defy anyone not to feel tender about that child.
The sentence that precedes all of this is doing so much work.
Eliot writes: "Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
"Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
As usual — those two words contain the entire biography of a misunderstood child.
They also quietly indict Tom — his imagination is always the limiting factor in their relationship.
The narrator's irony is so finely calibrated here — fond of Maggie, clear-eyed about the comedy, never condescending.
There's something important buried in the reason Maggie runs to the gypsies specifically.
She has been so often told she was like a gypsy, and half wild — those are the words used to manage her, to mark her as deviant.
"she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and 'half wild,' that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of escaping opprobrium"
She internalises the insult and tries to make it into a refuge.
That's not just a child's fantasy — that's a survival strategy for someone who has been told, repeatedly, that she doesn't belong.
And Tom, characteristically, rejected the gypsy plan because gypsies were thieves and hardly got anything to eat.
Tom's objections are always practical — he has no room for Maggie's larger scale.
And of course the fantasy collapses — rather spectacularly.
Eliot gives us a passage that is genuinely gothic — and genuinely funny — almost simultaneously.
The collapse of the gypsy fantasy is one of Eliot's great comic set-pieces, and it works because it follows its own internal logic so faithfully.
Maggie's imagination is expansive enough to escalate from welcome guest to potential cannibal victim in five minutes flat.
Listen to this: "she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking"
Gradual cooking. That qualifier is everything — it's the word of a child who has thought about this very carefully.
And then the theology kicks in — she wonders whether the Devil would know her thoughts.
That is such a beautifully observed child-brain — the switch from terror to doctrinal anxiety in a single sentence.
And what I find remarkable is that Eliot lets us laugh without ever making Maggie small.
The thing she most dreaded was to offend the gypsies by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them.
"the thing she most dreaded was to offend the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them"
Even while terrified she is managing social obligations — she is already practising the female art of concealment.
It's funny, yes — but it's also the first version of the bind that will define her entire life.
Caroline's right — and it connects directly to the passage about Maggie's education, which I find genuinely sharp.
Eliot describes a child who reads the dictionary because she has so few books — and from that, deduces what "poly" means.
Eliot's phrase for this is devastating in its precision.
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge"
Her small mind — not small in capacity, but small in resource.
This is a class analysis as much as a character sketch — what a girl with Maggie's mind would have become with access to proper education.
Her thoughts were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams — and the system made sure it stayed that way.
And Tom — who benefits from that education Maggie is denied — actually learns more from her questions than from his Latin lessons.
There's a beautiful irony in that passage about Tom missing Maggie at school.
That passage about Tom missing Maggie is one of the novel's most quietly generous moments.
Eliot doesn't let us simply resent Tom — she shows us his genuine grief, and then immediately shows us what he loses when she's gone.
Her questions about the Roman Empire — questions that Mr Stelling probably couldn't answer properly — opened up history for Tom.
Eliot renders this with that characteristic ironic tenderness.

"he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar"
A dim understanding — that is the exact, unglamourised measure of what Maggie gave him.
And it was more than the formal curriculum ever managed to give him.
What moves me about that passage is the phrase fetched away in the gig — it sounds so casual, so matter-of-fact.
She is fetched and carried like a parcel.
And then the study is once more quite lonely — Tom feels it, but it never seems to occur to him that Maggie might also feel something.
His learning, her absence — these things exist in adjacent boxes in his mind.
He grieved her, and yet he couldn't quite connect her presence with the brightness she brought.
I want to bring in the passage with Mr Tulliver, because it speaks to exactly this theme of confinement — but from a different angle.
Tulliver says to Maggie: "Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
That line contains the whole tragedy of the Tullivers in seven words.
He loves her — but his love can't remake the world, can't give her a second chance any more than it can give him one.
The hunger Maggie has — intellectual, emotional — it was never going to be fed by the world she was born into.
That line — I shall never live twice o'er — lands like a stone.
Eleanor, Caroline, Daniel — thank you.
We've been tracing the shape of Maggie's mind from childhood — the hunger, the imagination, the fantasy, and the confinement.
In our next segment, we'll follow her as she grows — and as the world begins to close around her in earnest.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers of this novel, and we're turning our attention to something that doesn't always get its due: George Eliot's wit.
Because The Mill on the Floss is often read as a tragic novel — and it is — but it is also ferociously funny.
With us is Dr Eleanor Hartley, who teaches creative writing and reads Eliot like a fellow novelist — always asking how the effects are built.
Dr Daniel Rosen brings the eye of a cultural historian — he sees every comic scene as also a document of class and power.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel for decades and reads passages aloud the way other people play music.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because you've always said Eliot's humour is inseparable from her tenderness.
Where do we feel that most in the early passages?
There's a passage I come back to again and again when I think about what Eliot does with childhood.
It's Tom and Maggie on one of their happy mornings by the Floss, and the narrator gives us their inner world with such precision that it becomes almost heartbreaking.
Listen to how she puts it:

"They trotted along and sat down together, with no thought that life would ever change much for them; they would only get bigger and not go to school, and it would always be like the holidays; they would always live together and be fond of each other."
That word "always" — it appears three times in those two sentences.
The children are insisting on permanence with the full confidence of people who have never lost anything.
And we know, because we've read this novel, that the river will take everything.
That is funny and devastating in the same breath.
What Caroline is pointing to is a very specific narrative technique — free indirect discourse pushed to its tenderly ironic extreme.
Eliot inhabits the children's consciousness completely — "they would only get bigger and not go to school" — that is genuinely how a child thinks.
But the narrator never disappears.
You feel this vast, knowing, sorrowful adult intelligence holding the children's certainty very gently — the way you'd hold a soap bubble.
The comedy is structural: the gap between what they believe and what we know.
Eliot builds that gap into every clause, and she does it without a single word of explicit irony.
I'd add that the idyll isn't just emotional — it's material.
The mill, the Ripple, the Floss — Tom thinks people are at a disadvantage who live anywhere else on the globe.
That's the small provincial landlord's worldview crystallised in a child — this place, this property, this river, as the natural centre of everything.
And it is funny — the earnest solipsism of it.
But Eliot is also recording the exact ideology that will destroy Maggie: the sense that these particular acres, this particular mill, define what a person's life means.
The comedy and the critique are the same gesture.
And then Eliot does something even sharper with Maggie, about ten chapters later.
This is the moment Maggie pushes Lucy into the mud — and Eliot frames it with this extraordinary mock-tragic commentary.
She writes:

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action; the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud."
"Pink-and-white Lucy" and "cow-trodden mud" — in the same sentence as Aristotelian tragedy.
It is one of the funniest sentences in Victorian fiction, and I mean that with complete seriousness.
The Greek is doing extraordinary work there.
Aristotle's term for the magnitude, the scale of action that tragedy requires — Eliot drops it into a scene of a small girl shoving her cousin.
The gap between the register of the language and the register of the event — that is the joke, and it's a sophisticated joke.
But here's what I love about Eliot's craft: she doesn't let the comedy dismiss Maggie's inner life.
She says there were passions at war — and she means it.
The tragedy is real; it simply cannot find its proper action in the confined world Maggie inhabits.
Exactly — the inadequacy of the action is the point.
Maggie's passionate nature has nowhere to go in St Ogg's.
The comedy is actually an indictment of a social world so narrow that a woman of tragic dimensions can only push someone into the mud.
What's funny about that sentence is also what's enraging about it.
Let's stay with that social world — because Eliot finds other comic targets in it besides Maggie.
Caroline, there's a scene with Bob Jakin and Mrs Glegg that you've called one of the great comic performances in the novel.
What's Bob actually doing when he's supposedly selling her that muslin?
Bob Jakin is a genius, and the scene is a masterclass in verbal sleight of hand.
He's ostensibly trying to sell Mrs Glegg figured muslin, but everything he says is designed to make her want it by convincing her it's beneath her.
He says:
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
He's telling her the muslin is too good for her to even contemplate — it would only frustrate her.
Then he flings it away dramatically, tells her it'll go to the huckster's wife at Fibb's End for ten shillings.
He's invented a rival buyer, invented an aristocratic provenance — the Princess Victoria apparently wore this fabric — and constructed the whole performance out of pure invention.
It's comedy, but Bob is also the smartest economist in the scene.
Bob is working with the only tools available to someone with no capital but wit.
He's a pedlar — he can't hold fixed stock, he can't afford to lose a sale, he has no institutional backing.
What he has is an exact map of his customer's vanity and class anxiety.
Mrs Glegg is terrified of being seen as less than her station.
Bob is selling her the fantasy of her own superiority, and the muslin is almost beside the point.
Eliot finds this funny, but she also finds it precise — it's an anatomy of how class operates as a set of performed desires.
And notice how Eliot renders Bob's dialect — it's not caricature, it's craft.
The dropped consonants, the rhythms — "it 'ud on'y take away your appetite" — that's a sentence with perfect comic timing built into its sounds.
Eliot respects Bob enough to give him his own verbal music.
He's not a figure of fun in the way a lesser novelist would make him — he's the most alive character in the scene.
Which brings us to Eliot's most ruthless comedy — and I think her most politically charged.
The passage in which St Ogg's society imagines how it would have received Maggie if she'd come back as Mrs Stephen Guest.
Caroline, how do you read that passage?
It's the passage I would give anyone who doubted that Eliot could write satire.
The narrator steps forward and says something terrifyingly direct:
"We judge others according to results; how else? — not knowing the process by which results are arrived at."
That "how else" is extraordinary — the narrator almost seems to excuse the behaviour before skewering it completely.
Then follows this extended ventriloquism of St Ogg's gossip — the voices tumbling over each other, the rationalizations piling up.
And at the very end, the poor Miss Unit who refuses to visit is suspected of not having received her invitation cards.
The one person with moral integrity is reduced to a social embarrassment.
The phrase "public opinion, in these cases, is always of the feminine gender" — that is a genuinely devastating observation about ideology and scapegoating.
Society projects its moral enforcement onto women — "the world's wife" does the judging, so the world keeps its hands clean.
And the comedy of the passage — the voices of St Ogg's gossiping — is funny precisely because it's so recognisable.
Eliot knew that the most effective critique is the one that makes you laugh and then makes you ashamed of laughing.
What I find extraordinary structurally is that Eliot gives the gossip directly — in quotation marks, in the voices of unnamed speakers.
"And a deformed young man, you know! — and young Guest so very fascinating."
The narrator hands the floor to St Ogg's and lets it condemn itself.
She doesn't editorialise — she doesn't need to.
The accumulation of petty calculation disguised as sympathy does all the work.
There's something almost novelistic in what you're all describing — Eliot using comedy as a form of moral intelligence rather than mere relief from the tragedy.
The wit is never decorative; it's always doing the sharpest critical work.
In our next segment, we're going to look at how that intelligence turns inward — how Eliot's narrator grapples with sympathy itself.
Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the show where we take George Eliot's great novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Today's segment goes to the heart of the novel: the bond between Maggie and Tom Tulliver, and the slow, aching rupture of that bond.
To explore it, I'm joined by three brilliant readers, each bringing a very different lens.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Eliot the way a watchmaker reads a movement — for the precision of every mechanism.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who finds in every domestic scene a register of class, power, and economic fate.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and feels its sentences in her bones.
Let's begin where Eliot herself begins — with the gravity of home.
What strikes me every time I return to the early chapters is how Eliot makes home into something almost metaphysical.
It isn't sentimentality — it's something far more precise than that.
She gives us this extraordinary passage about Tom returning home across the snow-covered bridge, and the narrator lifts it into a kind of philosophy of attachment.

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
That phrase — the labour of choice — quietly demolishes the Enlightenment idea that rational preference is how we build a self.
For Eliot, we are made before we choose — and that making is what Tom and Maggie share.
Caroline's exactly right about the philosophical weight, and I'd add that the craft here is audacious.
Eliot pivots mid-passage into a kind of mock-patriotic joke — about the British man distinguished from the foreign brute by his striving after better upholstery.
It's funny, and then it isn't — because she immediately turns that irony back against itself.
She sets up the quote setup with real care:
"if our affections had not a trick of twining round those old inferior things; if the loves and sanctities of our life had no deep immovable roots in memory."
Twining — such a careful word.
Not clinging, not grasping — twining, like a plant that grows around something over time, inseparably.
That's the structure of Tom and Maggie's bond — and it's also what makes the breach so devastating.
I want to sit with that word — inferior — because Eliot doesn't let it pass without notice.
The furniture of the Tulliver home would be scorned at auction.
The market's judgment is contemptuous — and yet Eliot argues that the market's judgment is precisely what must not govern our deepest attachments.
That's a quiet but serious argument against the logic of economic improvement — the very logic that will destroy the Tulliver family.
Mr Tulliver loses the mill because he cannot navigate a world where value is calculated in pounds and legal precedent rather than loyalty and labour.
And before he dies, he says something that breaks me every time.
"We shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
The world has defeated him — not through any personal moral failure, but through a system he was never equipped to fight.
That line undoes me every time I read it.
And what Eliot does around it is so deft — it's a man asking for a kiss, reaching for ordinary domestic peace, even in ruin.
That pulls Maggie into a particular kind of love — a love the narrator names precisely.
"That simple, primitive love which knits us to the beings who have been nearest to us, in their times of helplessness or of anguish."
Primitive — not in a diminishing sense, but in the sense of first.
It precedes argument, it precedes reason — and Eliot says quite plainly: it is supreme.
And yet — and this is where the novel becomes genuinely tragic — that same primitive bond is what Tom weaponises.
Eliot's narrator turns on Tom with an almost forensic coldness when she describes how his mind works.
It's one of the most devastating character portraits in the novel.
She describes minds that cannot tolerate complexity — and then she names what fills the void:

"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas."
A habitation — the same kind of habitation that home provides.
Eliot shows us that the very capacity for rootedness — the thing that made Tom and Maggie inseparable as children — becomes in Tom a closed system.
He inherits his father's hatred of Wakem, and he has no cognitive machinery to question it.
What's remarkable — and I think underappreciated — is how clearly Eliot sees that Tom's rigidity is socially produced.
His narrowness isn't a private character flaw — it's what this class, at this historical moment, needs its sons to be.
Duty, rectitude, the authority of the father's memory — these are not virtues in any abstract sense.
They are ideological tools — they tell Tom whom to exclude and on what grounds.
And the person excluded is Maggie — not for any wickedness, but for refusing to be contained.
And there's no one in St Ogg's who can hold the situation steady for Maggie — not even Dr Kenn, who genuinely tries.
Eliot gives us a beautiful and painful portrait of a good man completely paralysed.
He can see that Maggie's conscience is sound — and he knows he cannot touch it.
"Her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
He recognises moral integrity — and is powerless to protect the person who has it.
That, I think, is the novel's most searing argument: that goodness, without structural power, cannot save anyone.
What this conversation keeps circling is a paradox at the novel's core — that the same roots which nourish also bind.
Memory, home, family loyalty — the very things that make Maggie and Tom who they are also make reconciliation impossible.
In our next segment, we'll look at how Eliot uses the river — patient, indifferent, inevitable — to mirror that irresolvable tension.
Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into George Eliot's extraordinary novel — its craft, its comedy, its heartbreak.
With me are three readers who know this book as well as anyone could.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who lives for the architecture of great prose — the sentence that does three things at once.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of class and power — and who has very little patience for comfortable readings.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible way.
We begin with a segment we're calling Mill and Mist: Eliot's Craft — looking at how she constructs character and psychology through her prose.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Eliot announces her game.
There's a passage introducing Tom Tulliver — this apparently unremarkable boy — that is doing something quietly audacious.
She describes him as one of those lads who look as much alike as goslings — cream-and-roses, indeterminate features, utterly generic.
And then she pivots, and the pivot is everything.
She writes — and I want to read this exactly —
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
The ordinariness is the disguise, not the truth.
Tom's blank face is a kind of warning, if you know how to read it.
That passage is a masterclass in what I'd call the narrator's double game.
On the surface she's describing Tom's appearance — but she's actually constructing an argument about how we misread people.
Notice the personification — Nature doesn't just produce Tom, she conceals her intentions inside him.
Nature has, she says, "deep cunning which hides itself under the appearance of openness."
That phrase — deep cunning — applies equally to Nature, to Tom, and to the narrator herself.
Eliot is telling us, with considerable relish, how her own novel works.
I want to stay with that passage, because there's a dimension Caroline and Eleanor have circled that deserves naming directly.
Eliot writes that the dark-eyed, rebellious girl may after all turn out to be a passive being compared with this pink-and-white bit of masculinity.
She's not just talking about temperament — she's talking about the social machinery that will shape both children differently.
Tom's inflexibility will be rewarded by a world built for men like him.
Maggie's expressiveness — her very vividness — will be punished by that same world.
Eliot frames it as Nature's irony, but she knows perfectly well it is society's machinery.
Daniel's point makes the later scene with Mr Tulliver all the more devastating.
He's ridden away from his sister's farm — all resolve and forward motion — and then something stops him.
He sits on his horse in that deep-rutted lane, turning his head from side to side — Eliot says — in a melancholy way.
And then he speaks aloud — to no one.
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
It's barely nine words of direct speech, and it breaks your heart.
He loves her fiercely and cannot protect her, and he knows it.
What Eliot does structurally in that scene is extraordinary.
The whole passage has been about Mr Tulliver's impulsiveness — his tendency to act first and think later.
Eliot has this wonderful description of him earlier — the narrator says, in the driest possible voice —
"for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread."
That's a diagnosis and a joke in the same breath.
But then that same impulsive man halts in the lane and speaks his grief aloud — and suddenly we're nowhere near comedy.
The tonal shift is brutal, and it's entirely deliberate.
There's something else in that scene that I think we should sit with.
Mr Tulliver has just been riding to call in a debt from his sister's husband — a man, we understand, who can barely afford it.
He's doing it because he owes money to Mrs Glegg — and his pride cannot bear the appearance of financial difficulty.
So the machinery of debt cascades down the family — from the Gleggs to Tulliver to the Mosses.
And it's in the middle of this financial manoeuvre that grief about Maggie ambushes him.
Eliot refuses to let the economic and the emotional live in separate compartments.
They are the same life.
That phrase — the same life — feels like a way into everything we'll be discussing today.
The economic and the emotional, the comic and the tragic — in Eliot they are never as separate as we might like.
We'll carry that thought forward as we continue unpacking The Mill on the Floss.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today's segment is called The Economy of the Heart — and we mean that quite literally.
We're asking how George Eliot tracks the way human feeling circulates — or fails to — between people who desperately need it.
With me today are three readers who have thought hard about this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how fiction is actually built — the sentences, the structures, the images that do the quiet heavy lifting.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of power — and George Eliot, he'll argue, drew those maps with uncomfortable precision.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence and brings to it a reader's intimate, hard-won love.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because I think you see something in the way Eliot handles childhood enmity that most readers miss entirely.
Yes — and I think it matters that Eliot frames this not as a personal failing but as a structural inevitability.
Tom and Philip's brief warmth during Tom's illness — that moment of shared vulnerability — dissolves the instant the crisis passes.
And Eliot gives us the reason in the form of a metallurgical metaphor that I find almost brutal in its clarity.
"If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out."
The word 'welded' is doing enormous work there.
Sympathy requires compatible material — and the social formations that have made Tom into a Tulliver and Philip into a Wakem have already determined the composition.
The boys don't choose hostility. It has been manufactured for them by their fathers' enmity, by class position, by the whole architecture of St. Ogg's.
What I love about that metaphor is how it converts emotion into matter — literally into metal.
Eliot is writing here as an omniscient narrator who will not let sentiment soften her diagnosis.
Notice she doesn't say 'they grew apart.' She says they 'inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out.'
That word 'inevitably' is load-bearing. It forecloses all possibility of individual agency rescuing the situation.
The narrator is almost coldly generous — she sees more than the characters ever could, and what she sees is not consoling.
And yet — and I want to hold onto this — there's an extraordinary tenderness even inside that cold analysis.
When Mr. Tulliver warns Tom about Philip, he says, 'He's a poor crooked creature, and takes after his dead mother.'
There's genuine pity in that — misguided, freighted with prejudice — but it's not cruelty.
And yet in the very next breath he warns Tom: 'Don't you be getting too thick with him; he's got his father's blood in him too.'
Pity and suspicion in the same sentence. That's the world of this novel in miniature.
Exactly — and the cruelty of it is that Tulliver's warning has the structure of common sense.
It's prudential wisdom dressed up as paternal care. And it works — because the world it describes is real.
The gray colt does kick like his black sire — meaning Tom will suffer from Philip's father's actions, and he knows it.
So the prejudice is also a form of realism. Which makes it almost impossible to argue against from inside the novel's world.
That tension — between what's emotionally true and what's structurally determined — runs very deep in Eliot's portrayal of Maggie.
Daniel, you've been looking closely at a passage that I think is one of the most quietly devastating in the entire novel.
It's the passage where young Maggie runs upstairs in tears — and what Eliot does with it is extraordinary.
The surface narrative is a child being upset. The narrator's intervention turns it into a philosophical crisis about the nature of early suffering.
Listen to how Eliot frames this.

"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present."
'The blind sufferer's present.' That phrase indicts every adult who has ever dismissed a child's grief as temporary.
And notice the class dimension: Maggie's hunger for love is inseparable from 'poverty and the companionship of her mother's narrow griefs.'
Her emotional deprivation and her material deprivation are the same deprivation. Eliot refuses to separate them.
That passage always stops me completely. Every time.
What Eliot captures is the specific texture of childhood despair — the way it fills the entire present because there's no future yet to console with.
'The soul is made up of wants.' That's almost unbearably precise about what it feels like to be Maggie at that age.
And then — 'the world outside the books was not a happy one.' Books have been her whole alternative world.
And now even that gap between the world of books and the world of St. Ogg's is registered as a kind of grief.
The narratorial shift in that passage is worth pausing on technically.
We move from free indirect discourse — 'Everybody in the world seemed so hard and unkind to Maggie' — deep inside her consciousness.
And then suddenly Eliot pivots: 'though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair.'
That 'we' is a structural move of remarkable audacity. The narrator steps forward and implicates the reader directly.
We are the ones who look on and think lightly. Eliot is accusing us — gently, but unmistakably.
That implication of the reader connects to something that becomes much more fraught later in the novel — the question of how we judge Maggie.
And specifically how Tom judges her. Daniel, the passage you've been sitting with from the confrontation scene is I think one of Eliot's most forensic pieces of moral anatomy.
It is — and what makes it so devastating is precisely the evenhandedness of Eliot's scalpel.
She doesn't let Maggie off; she shows her 'writhing under the demonstrable truth' of Tom's charge.
But then she turns the same cold eye on Tom — and this is where Eliot becomes something close to ruthless.

"He did not know how much of an old boyish repulsion and of mere personal pride and animosity was concerned in the bitter severity of the words by which he meant to do the duty of a son and a brother."
'He meant to do the duty.' Eliot gives Tom full credit for his sincerity — and then demolishes its foundations.
The sentence that follows is the key: 'Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind.'
The inability to examine one's own motives is presented not as wickedness but as a structural limitation — a kind of trained incapacity produced by the values of his world.
That phrase — 'matters of an intangible kind' — is doing so much.
Tom's entire world is the world of tangible things: debts, obligations, land, reputation.
Motive, feeling, the complexity of another person's inner life — those are precisely what he cannot see or value.
And Eliot shows us that this is not stupidity. It's a kind of epistemological consequence of being Tom Tulliver — of being made the way his world made him.
The novel has terrible compassion for Tom. Which makes his cruelty to Maggie all the harder to forgive.
I think about that line — 'Tom had his terrible clutch on her conscience and her deepest dread' — and what it means for Maggie to live under that.
She can't dismiss him. She can't simply say he's wrong. Because he's partially right — and she knows it.
Her 'whole soul rebelled against it as unfair from its incompleteness.' That word — incompleteness — is so precisely chosen.
Tom can only see the action. He cannot see the struggle behind it, the years of striving, the weight of what she has already given up.
And so his truth is true — and also a lie. And Maggie has to carry both of those things simultaneously. That's the unbearable part.
Which brings us to the passage that I think is the summit of all of this — Maggie's internal battle in the Stephen Guest chapters.
Daniel, this is where all those earlier formations — the trained incapacity for self-examination, the poverty of love, the clutch of conscience — converge in Maggie.
Yes — and what Eliot is doing here is almost audacious in its honesty.
She says directly: 'it seemed to her as if all the worst evil in her had lain in ambush till now, and had suddenly started up full-armed.'
This is not Maggie as sentimental heroine. This is Maggie as a site of genuine moral conflict — with the selfish impulse given its full weight and name.
'She had had to suffer through many years of her life; and who had renounced anything for her?' That question is the most dangerous sentence in the novel.
Because it's unanswerable. Nobody has renounced anything for Maggie. The world has taken from her constantly and given almost nothing back.
And yet. Eliot gives us the counter-movement — the 'old voices making themselves heard with rising power.'
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
'The best organs of her soul.' Eliot makes sympathy and faith into physical equipment — as essential as feet. You cannot walk without them.
That metaphor is one of the great sentences in Victorian fiction — and it's great because it's so bodily.
Eliot doesn't say 'she would diminish herself morally.' She says she would be maiming herself — physically disabled.
And notice the parallelism: 'maiming her feet' — 'maiming the faith and sympathy.' The grammatical structure enacts the equation.
The body and the soul are written as syntactic equals. That's a theological claim made through sentence architecture.
What moves me most in that whole passage is the description of Maggie's outward appearance — 'quiescence and even torpor of manner.'
Lucy sees depression on the surface. She cannot see the 'fierce battle of emotions' underneath.
And Eliot says this is 'such as Maggie in all her life of struggle had never known or foreboded.'
All her previous suffering was preparation. This is the real thing — and nobody around her can see it happening.
That's the loneliness that runs through everything in this novel. The most important things happen inside people, and no one can see them.
The loneliness of interiority — that's a beautiful way to hold all of this together.

From Tom and Philip discovering they are made of incompatible metal, to young Maggie weeping in a world that cannot see her wants, to the adult Maggie fighting a battle that nobody around her knows is being fought.
The economy of this novel is brutal: feeling is expended constantly, and almost none of it is returned at the right rate, to the right person, at the right time.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how the novel's final catastrophe arises directly from these accumulated deficits — the flood as reckoning.
We've ranged widely today — from the architecture of memory to the machinery of class, from the river's pull to the schoolroom's cruelties.
Before we close, I want to bring us back to where the novel itself begins — and ends — with an act of submergence.
Eleanor, you've been sitting with that extraordinary opening passage — the one where the narrator wakes from a dream.
What does it mean that the entire novel is framed as a reverie someone has just dozed off into?
It's one of the most disarming openings in all of Victorian fiction, and I think we underestimate how radical it is.
George Eliot constructs what looks like a realist establishing scene — a mill, a river, a winter afternoon — and then pulls the rug from under it entirely.
Listen to how she does it — this is the narrator speaking directly to us:

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
That "Ah" — so sudden, so physical — it's not a rhetorical flourish, it's a body coming back to itself.
The entire opening — the mill, the frost, the child on the bank — has been a dream inside a chair inside a book.
And yet it felt utterly real a moment ago.
What strikes me every time I re-read that moment is the intimacy of it — the narrator turning to us as though we're sitting in the same room.
"Before I dozed off, I was going to tell you" — there's something almost confessional about that phrasing.
The novel begins with an apology for getting lost in memory.
And then — and this is what moves me — the whole book that follows is that same condition, extended across hundreds of pages.
We are all pressing our elbows on the arms of our chairs as we read it.
I want to connect that framing to something we saw deep in the novel — in the schoolroom, of all places.
Because the novel's tenderness toward memory isn't only the narrator's — it belongs to the children too, and it costs them.
That passage where Tom, broken down over Latin supines for the fifth time, turns to prayer — it's devastating precisely because it's so private.
He has no other resource left.
And so he adds, in the same low whisper as his proper prayers:
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
A child addressing God about supines.
That is what the system has reduced him to — prayer as a last, desperate study aid.
And notice what Eliot does structurally there — she tells us exactly what the prayer is, word for word.
She grants Tom the dignity of being heard precisely when the adult world refuses to hear him at all.
The narrator's act of remembering — which we saw in that opening reverie — is also an act of moral attention.
To dream back into the past, to press your elbows on the chair — it is, for Eliot, the work of justice as much as nostalgia.
And then he worries about Euclid — whether to pray for understanding, or for some other mental state more applicable to the case.
That little parenthetical hesitation — it's both funny and heartbreaking in the same breath.
He settles on asking Mr Stelling to simply stop assigning it.
"And make Mr Stelling say I sha'n't do Euclid any more. Amen."
There it is — a child's theology, perfectly logical on its own terms, utterly without guile.
What I keep returning to is how much Eliot trusts these small, private moments to carry the novel's largest argument.
Tom's prayer isn't a comic digression — it is the indictment.
A system that grinds a boy's natural strengths to nothing and leaves him whispering to God about grammar — that system is not incidental to the tragedy.
It is the tragedy.
A reverie in an armchair, and a whispered prayer against Euclid — two kinds of helplessness reaching toward something just out of reach.
That feels like a fitting place to leave The Mill on the Floss today.
My thanks to Dr Eleanor Hartley, Dr Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — for a conversation that was, I think, as rich as the novel deserves.
The Mill on the Floss Unpacked will return.
Until then — keep pressing your elbows on the chair.

Maggie went up to her own room to pour out all that indignant remonstrance,
against which Tom’s mind was close barred, in bitter tears. Then, when
the first burst of unsatisfied anger was gone by, came the recollection of that
quiet time before the pleasure which had ended in to-day’s misery had
perturbed the clearness and simplicity of her life. She used to think in that
time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene
heights above worldly temptations and conflict. And here she was down again in
the thick of a hot strife with her own and others’ passions. Life was not
so short, then, and perfect rest was not so near as she had dreamed when she
was two years younger. There was more struggle for her, and perhaps more
falling. If she had felt that she was entirely wrong, and that Tom had been
entirely right, she could sooner have recovered more inward harmony; but now
her penitence and submission were constantly obstructed by resentment that
would present itself to her no otherwise than as a just indignation. Her heart
bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him
with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost
like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and
tighten her fingers on her palm.

Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had

previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
